title: Modeling Asymmetries in Be Star Disks Using Spectro-interferometric H-alpha Observations from the CHARA Array's VEGA Instrument
summary: Be stars are rapidly rotating B-type stars with outflowing decretion disks. The observational record shows that in many cases the peaks of their H$α$ flux profile vary on long timescales. These changes are probably caused by the development of disk brightness asymmetries that are related to global disk oscillation modes. Here we present spectro-interferometric observations made with the CHARA Array interferometer and the VEGA beam combiner that document the interferometric data across the H$α$ line for the Be stars $γ$ Cas, $φ$ Per, $ζ$ Tau, and $β$ CMi. The differential interferometric visibility amplitudes and phases across the H$α$ emission line reveal clues about the asymmetries present in their disks. Here we describe a model of the H$α$ formation that calculates the emission intensity at spatial positions around the star and disk. The parameters describing the disk and the oscillation mode are optimized to match the interferometric data and contemporaneous H$α$ spectroscopy. The analysis confirms the presence of strong disk asymmetries at the time of the observations (2020) in the cases of $γ$ Cas and $φ$ Per, and hints that weaker oscillation modes were also present in the disks of $ζ$ Tau and $β$ CMi. The success of this single epoch study demonstrates the promise of future interferometric programs to investigate how the modes precess within the disk and grow and decline over time.

title: Magnetic vector potentials and helicity in periodic domains
summary: For a magnetic field in three-dimensional Euclidean space, we argue about the existence of a magnetic vector potential in a finite cuboid with periodic boundary conditions. We first argue in physical terms by representing periodic domains as tori and show that in some cases, the generating electric current is unphysical. We then represent magnetic fields and vector potentials as differential 2 and 1-forms. For a given magnetic field we ask the question whether a corresponding vector potential exists. Singly periodic domains are shown to always allow for a vector potential. For doubly periodic domains it only exists if the net magnetic flux through the non-periodic dimension vanishes, while for triply periodic domains the net flux must vanish in all directions. This has implications for the definition of magnetic helicity in periodic domains. We show that periodic domains together with a mean magnetic flux lead to contradicting results about the value of the magnetic helicity and we show in a few thought experiments fundamental contradictions to the interpretation as the linking of magnetic field lines. For the helicity we can even construct magnetic fields in periodic domains for which the magnetic helicity exists, but the calculations of the magnetic helicity do not lead to meaningful results due to the gauge freedom. With that we conclude that in presence of a mean magnetic field the calculated magnetic helicity cannot be interpreted geometrically in a straightforward way. However, using the winding gauge we can recover the geometric interpretation of the helicity as the flux averaged magnetic field line winding. Finally, for the solar relevant non-periodic domain with finite point-wise flux and zero integrated flux, using an appropriate gauge transformation the magnetic helicity can be shown to vanish. The winding helicity, however, would lead to a non-vanishing value here.

title: Accretor Luminosity as Probe of Orbital Evolution and Magnetic Braking in AM CVn Binaries
comment: 33 pages (including 6 pages of Appendix), 14 figures; Under review in ApJ
summary: AM CVn binaries are ultracompact systems with orbital periods $P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 70$ min, where a white dwarf accretes from a He-rich semidegenerate donor. At short orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 20$ min), rapid accretion reheats the accretor. As the system widens and the mass transfer rate decreases, the accretor follows standard white dwarf cooling at longer orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \gtrsim 30$ min). The accretor cooling luminosity then acts as a powerful probe into the orbital evolution of the binary. Recent observations show that the accretor appears brighter (younger) at long orbital periods, compared to models where orbital angular momentum loss is solely set by gravitational wave emission. We show that additional angular momentum loss, which we ascribe to magnetic braking of the donor, can better reproduce observations of accretor luminosity. We test and constrain various proposed magnetic braking formalisms, for the white dwarf, helium star, and evolved cataclysmic variable (CV) channels for AM CVn formation. None of the magnetic braking formalisms in their original form can reproduce the observations, but the widely popular magnetic braking proposed by Rappaport et al. 1983 boosted by a factor $\approx 5$, or the saturated magnetic braking proposed by Matt et al. 2015 boosted by a factor of $\approx 150$, yields satisfactory results. We also find that the CARB formalism, recently applied to the evolved CV channel, is strongly in tension with observations of accretor luminosity. Our models motivate UV spectroscopy observations, and dedicated WD atmosphere models for AM CVn accretors.

title: Precise Radii of Visual Binaries with Dynamical Masses: $ξ$ Bootis $\&$ 70 Ophiuchi
comment: 26 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: A new orbital solution for $ξ$ Bootis (GJ 566 AB, P=152 yrs) and the recently revised orbital solution for 70 Ophiuchi (GJ 702 AB, P=88 yrs) yield component masses precise to 0.4\%. Their relatively wide separations ($>0.4^{\prime\prime}$) allow the components to be studied independently, making them ideal for testing the predictions of stellar evolutionary models. We use the six-telescope near-infrared MIRC-X and MYSTIC beam combiners at the CHARA Array to measure the angular diameters of all 4 stars. Combined with precise Gaia DR3 parallax values and bolometric fluxes, these interferometric measurements translate to stellar radii that are precise to $<2.4\%$ and effective temperatures precise to $<1.7\%$. We compare the measured radii and temperatures to four stellar evolutionary models (Lyon, Dartmouth, PARSEC, MIST). Over the mass range $0.67 - 0.91$ M$_\odot$, all models reproduce the observed properties within a few standard deviations, with no systematic offsets. The pairs are coeval and consistent with independent age estimates, further validating model predictions. With physical separations greater than 20 au, these pairs show no evidence of radius inflation, despite being spectroscopically classified as chromospherically active, and in the case of $ξ$ Bootis, probable members of the adolescent age ($\sim 0.4$ Gyr) Ursa Majoris Moving Group. In contrast, a set of 21 short-period ($P\lesssim$ 10 days) eclipsing binary stars with similar dynamical masses and metallicities are larger and often cooler than these same model predictions. Within this mass range, radius inflation appears to be associated with short-period binary star systems.

title: Ultraviolet Observations of Solar Active Phenomena
comment: 71 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in Space Sci. Rev
summary: Ultraviolet observations of the Sun have revolutionized our understanding of the structure and dynamics of the solar atmosphere. From the chromosphere all the way to the corona, there are ubiquitous jets due to magnetic reconnection and associated with type III radio bursts. Sporadic flares occur in the corona, representing an inevitable breakup of magnetic energy accumulation as new magnetic flux continues to pump into the solar atmosphere, which is further shuffled by solar surface motions. Once large-scale eruptions occur, magnetized plasmas are expelled out into the interplanetary space, leaving globally propagating waves and the following dimmings. The waves can be utilized to diagnose the coronal magnetic field which cannot be measured directly, and the dimmings can be used to estimate the ejected mass of eruptions and magnetic connectivity. Extreme ultraviolet spectroscopic observations provide information on the fractionation of different chemical elements, in particular those elements with low first ionization potential. Thanks to the high spatial resolution of solar observations, all these results are believed to shed light on our understanding of the activity on other stars which cannot be imaged.

title: Interstellar extinction estimates for nearly 90 million stars based on synthetic photometry from Gaia XP spectra
comment: Accepted for publication in New Astronomy. 11 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables
summary: Accurate stellar extinction measurements are essential for recovering intrinsic stellar properties and investigating the three-dimensional distribution of interstellar dust. We present reddening estimates for 87,270,425 stars using synthetic SMSS gri photometry derived from corrected Gaia DR3 XP spectra, combined with Gaia BP and RP, 2MASS JHKs, and WISE W1 photometry. Stellar extinction is determined through empirical SED fitting based on reference stellar loci constructed separately for dwarfs and giants. Comparisons with three external extinction catalogs show good overall agreement, with dispersions of 0.049-0.075 mag in E(B-V). The catalog covers approximately 99.99% of the sky. Using stars with sigma_d/d < 0.2, we further construct reddening maps in four distance ranges from 0 to 5 kpc, revealing prominent molecular clouds and large-scale Galactic dust structures. Extinction-corrected color-absolute-magnitude diagrams show significantly tighter stellar sequences and consistent red-clump features in different Galactic fields. The resulting catalog provides a homogeneous data set for stellar extinction correction and studies of Galactic dust structure.

title: Characterising stellar photometry with invertible neural networks: Joint inference of stellar parameters and extinction
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures, 1 table, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We introduce an extension to a simulation-based deep-learning approach for the characterisation of stellar photometry and investigate the feasibility of jointly estimating stellar properties and extinction. We used the PARSEC stellar evolutionary models to train a conditional invertible neural network (cINN) to jointly estimate full posterior distributions of stellar parameters and extinction. We tested our cINN on synthetic data and real Gaia+2MASS photometry of the two star-forming regions Taurus and Upper Scorpius. We compared our predicted extinction maps to two independent catalogues based on Gaia XP-spectra. On synthetic test data, our trained cINN exhibited a good predictive performance, achieving root mean squared errors (RMSEs) for the maximum a posteriori point estimates of about 0.16 mag for $A_V$, 0.07 dex for $\log(T_{eff}/K)$, 0.16 dex for $\log(g/cms^{-2})$, 0.2 dex for $\log(L/L\odot)$ and 0.1 dex for $\log(M_{ini}/M_\odot)$. Only $\log(age/yr)$ has proven harder to constrain with an RMSE of 0.56 dex. On the Gaia+2MASS observations of Taurus and Upper Scorpius, we retrieved reasonable extinction maps, exhibiting structures that are visually consistent with local clouds. Compared to the independent XP-spectra-based extinction studies, we found a good qualitative agreement and recovered the same prominent spatial structures. Quantitatively, however, we identified an average systematic overestimation of extinction in our approach of 0.5-0.7 mag compared to the spectroscopic studies. We investigated these offsets and identified photometric and distance uncertainties, which are currently unaccounted for in our approach, as likely causes. In conclusion, we demonstrated the feasibility of jointly estimating stellar parameters and extinction with our cINN approach, making it a promising avenue to further pursue for robust and efficient analysis of large photometric surveys.

title: Characterisation of B-type stars in four young Galactic open clusters. II. Photometric variability with TESS and identification of pulsating stars
summary: Pulsations and binarity are important properties of massive stars and influence their structure and evolution. Young open clusters are ideal laboratories to study massive stars, since they are mostly coeval and chemically homogeneous. We analyse 82 B-type stars in the Galactic open clusters $h$ and $χ$ Persei, NGC 457, NGC 581, and NGC 1960, which have ages between 15 and 30 Myr. We extract light curves using both simple aperture photometry and a point-spread-function-based method that minimises contamination from crowded fields in full-frame images from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. We successfully extract light curves for 63 stars. The majority have photometric variability caused by pulsations, showing how pulsations are a common property of young B-type stars in clusters. We classify stars into different pulsator types based on their spectral type and frequency spectrum. The most common pulsator class are beta Cephei stars, with 29 stars in total, and we discover pulsation modes in almost all stars with a spectral type of B2 or earlier. All Be stars show pulsations, which supports the consensus of the ubiquity of pulsations in these stars. Finally, we confirm that the majority of early B-type stars are in binary systems, except for two pulsating Be stars and a star with rotational modulation. This indicates that pulsations do not significantly bias the spectroscopic detection of short-period binaries, except for Be stars where the spectroscopic radial velocity variability threshold should be higher than the typical value of 20 km s$^{-1}$.

title: Atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances of young stars with APOGEE -- II. Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen, and Sulphur abundances in Orion
comment: 22 pages, 6 Figures, 6 Tables. Accepted in MNRAS
summary: We derived the abundances of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur, and iron in young G-, K-, and M-type stars (effective temperatures of 3500--5900 K) using APOGEE-2 infrared spectra. Our final sample comprises 195 slow rotators ($v\sin i$ $\leq$ 30 km~s$^{-1}$) in the Orion complex (Orion A, B, OB1, and $λ$~Ori). The abundances were determined using MARCS model atmospheres, atmospheric parameters derived with \tona, and the \bacc\ code. We obtained median abundances of $ε$(C) = 8.37$\pm$0.10, $ε$(N) = 7.35$\pm$0.16, $ε$(O) = 8.63$\pm$0.08, $ε$(S) = 7.19$\pm$0.18, and $ε$(Fe) = 7.45$\pm$0.05. Nitrogen is subsolar ([N/H] $=-0.48$), whereas carbon, oxygen, sulphur, and iron are within 0.1 dex of the solar values. We find no spatial structure within the Orion subgroups, and the only significant difference is a 0.29 dex lower nitrogen abundance in Orion A than in Orion OB1, which does not extend to the other elements. Compared with 430 nearby main-sequence stars analysed in the same way, Orion shows carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen abundances lower by 0.1--0.2 dex, although consistent within the errors, whereas sulphur and iron differ by less than 0.07 dex. We also compare our abundances with nebular abundances of HII regions and star-forming galaxies: the stellar abundances of oxygen, sulphur, and iron are higher, with the largest offset in iron, although the agreement in abundance ratios improves when temperature inhomogeneities and dust depletion are taken into account.

title: Recovering buoyancy-glitch parameters in low-luminosity red giants from global stellar properties with machine learning
summary: Buoyancy glitches in red giants provide localized information on the interior structure near the base of the convective envelope, but their properties are typically inferred from dedicated seismic modelling rather than global properties, limiting large-sample applications. We investigate whether the buoyancy-glitch amplitude ($A_g$), location ($W_{\rm g}^{\star}$), and width ($D_g$) can be recovered from global stellar properties using gradient-boosted tree regressors (XGBoost and LightGBM). The models were trained on a grid of 12580 synthetic stellar models of low-luminosity red giants, with target parameters derived from fits to the local buoyancy frequency profile. We find that $W_{\rm g}^{\star}$ and $D_g$ exhibit excellent recoverability, achieving test-set $\mathcal{R}^2$ values of 0.98 and 0.97, respectively. In contrast, $A_g$ shows moderate recoverability overall ($\mathcal{R}^2=0.68$). This reduced recoverability of $A_g$ is concentrated in the large frequency separation range $Δν= 4.6$--$18.9\,μ$Hz, where the glitch resides in the evanescent-zone transition between the convective envelope and the gravity-mode cavity, increasing intrinsic scatter. SHAP analysis shows that $ν_{\rm max}$ and $T_{\rm eff}$ dominate the predictions across all targets, indicating that the regressors rely primarily on evolutionary state. While $W_{\rm g}^{\star}$ and $D_g$ are tightly constrained by global evolutionary trends, the lower recoverability of $A_g$ reflects localized structural complexity associated with red-giant evolution. Overall, for the synthetic grid adopted here, these results indicate that global properties provide a direct estimate of the buoyancy-glitch parameters and a way to prioritise dedicated mixed-mode inversions for large asteroseismic samples such as Kepler and PLATO.
